NodeClosure {authorities, definitions, graphContentHash, ok, revisionId}; NodeClosureUnknown {authority:"NONE", code, detail, layer, ok:false, outcome:"UNKNOWN", upstream|null}; NodeClosureEntry {definition, nodeAuthorityHash, ok}.

COMPOSITION, zero authority minted: readCurrentNodeClosure calls readCurrentActiveGraph and, on ok, projects content.nodeAuthority + graphContentHash + revisionId. No re-derivation, no spec-file read, no caller input, no store write. The module doc names WHY in the terms step 1 measured — bindAuthority's encode-time re-derivation (GRAPH_CONTENT_AUTHORITY_DISAGREEMENT) and readGraphBody's identity check (GRAPH_BODY_IDENTITY_MISMATCH) are the integrity gates, and a reader-side copy would be free to drift from the first and would shadow the codec's vocabulary where no codec test looks.

PASSTHROUGH: on refusal the projection's code is returned UNCHANGED and upstream carries {code, layer, sourceCode, sourceLayer} — all four, so the graph-body layer's own attribution survives one more hop. Never restamped, never flattened.

TWO IMPLEMENTATION DECISIONS WORTH THE RECORD:
1. nodeClosureOf looks up BOTH halves BY KEY (two .find calls), not by a shared index. Index lookup would have been one call cheaper and is correct while the codec keeps the arrays aligned — but if alignment ever broke it would answer a NEIGHBOURING node's authority hash, which is the one failure a per-node accessor must not have. I chose the by-key form over adding an alignment guard deliberately: a guard there would be an unreachable branch (readAuthoritySection already requires index-aligned strictly-ascending arrays), and an unreachable refusal is a worse artifact than a redundant lookup. The suite still pins alignment separately as an observable property.
2. deepFreeze is the reader's own, applied to the whole ok result. The caller holds a view of sealed durable content; a mutable one lets a consumer edit a closure and pass it on as authority. It is idempotent, so it costs nothing if the codec already froze.
